newsitem.title: UK: Major says no chance of Britain leaving EU.
newsitem.headline: Major says no chance of Britain leaving EU.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major delivered a rebuke on Tuesday to anti-European Conservatives who have hampered his efforts to boost his flagging party, saying there was no reason for Britain to quit the European Union.

In the first of a series of presidential-style news conferences designed to bolster his waning election hopes, Major also hammered home a campaign message that a victory for the opposition Labour Party when the nation votes this year would mean "tears".
"The economic outlook is extremely bright. It would be very foolish indeed were that to be thrown away," he said.
"We have a choice economically between smiles and tears. I hope and believe when the election comes that people will choose the smiles and avoid the tears."
The Conservatives, who have won four elections in a row, are some 20 points behind the revamped Labour Party in opinion polls.
Major's Conservatives are portraying Labour as a "leap in the dark" for Britons, saying it represents a dangerous unknown and would be reckless with the economy.

But the surveys show voters are not yet buying Major's message that the Labour Party, dragged from the left to the political centre by its new leader, Tony Blair, would be disastrous for Britain's booming economy.

The Conservatives, portrayed by Labour as riddled with scandal and out of touch after 17 years in power, are dogged by infighting over the European Union. Many of its members of parliament demand a tougher line against Brussels to save their seats in the election, which must be held by May 22.

Major refused to bow to the "Eurosceptics" in his party who want a new, hard line on EU integration, saying: "I don't believe when you examine the implications of leaving the European Union that there is any remotely plausible case to be made for leaving...
"Of course we must stay in the European Union."
He used the conference, an early shot in the undeclared election campaign, to spotlight the three issues he wants to focus on -- the economy, Europe and constitutional reform.

Labour and the small opposition Liberal Democrats are discussing sweeping changes to Britain's constitution, including a bill of rights, parliaments for Scotland and Wales and possibly even the adoption of proportional representation.

Major said the Conservatives were not opposed to constitutional change. But he accused Labour and the small opposition Liberal Democrat Party of proposing "foolhardy" and "extremely damaging" changes simply for the sake of being different.
He warned that Labour would find it hard to make the kind of tough economic decisions he said were responsible for Britain's buoyant economic performance.
"I very much doubt that our political opponents would have taken those decisions in the first place," said Major, adding that a Labour victory would mean higher taxes and unemployment.
"It will need difficult decisions in the future just as in the past to maintain that prosperity."
